content: This article discusses the use of sign language as a means of communication with infants and toddlers. Development In the United States, the practice of teaching sign language to hearing infants and toddlers in non-signing families was pioneered by Linda Acredolo, a professor emeritus of psychology at the University of California, Davis, and Susan Goodwyn, a professor of psychology at California State University, Stanislaus. Joseph Garcia, an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter and a prominent advocate for using ASL with infants and toddlers, began his work in this field with his graduate thesis in 1986. His research focused on the role of sign language in early childhood language acquisition. Garcia's findings revealed that infants exposed to signs regularly and consistently starting at six to seven months of age could begin using signs effectively by the time they are eight or nine months old. Purpose Advocates of infant sign language believe that while infants and toddlers have a strong desire to communicate their needs and wishes, they are often unable to do so clearly due to the developmental lag in speech production. Speech requires the simultaneous coordination of the lips, tongue, breath, and vocal cords, which develops more slowly than cognitive abilities during the first months and years of life. This gap between the desire to communicate and the ability to do so often results in frustration and tantrums before children are capable of producing intelligible speech. Vocabulary Proponents of infant sign language have identified two primary categories of signs: need-based signs and highly motivating signs. Need-based Signs Need-based signs are used to express basic needs such as drink, food, sleepy, hot, cold, or change me. For example, the sign for drink or thirst can be demonstrated by mimicking the action of drinking from a bottle. Similarly, the sign for eating can be expressed by mimicking the motion of eating or by rubbing one's stomach. Highly Motivating Signs Highly motivating signs are focused on items or activities that are of interest or entertainment to the child, such as doggy, toy, or friend. Parents can encourage the expansion of their child's vocabulary by teaching signs for objects or activities that the child desires or seeks out. Systems Indigenous Sign Languages This method involves using vocabulary from the indigenous sign language of the region. For instance, in Australia, signs are adopted from Auslan (Australian Sign Language), while in the United States, ASL (American Sign Language) signs are used. This approach provides a standardized vocabulary that allows others to communicate with the baby using these signs. It also lays the foundation for the child to continue studying the indigenous sign language as they grow older. Home-based Sign Language Home-based sign language refers to a system of signs developed individually between the infant and their caregivers. Advocates of this approach argue that vocabulary from ASL or other formal sign languages may be too complex for an infant to produce effectively. In Popular Culture In the film Meet the Fockers, the character Jack (played by Robert De Niro) teaches his grandson, Little Jack, to communicate using sign language. The twins who portrayed Little Jack (Bradley and Spencer Pickren) learned sign language by watching Signing Time. videos.
